name: SIGMA - SSH Session Cadence Brute-Force Indicator (Zeek ssh.log) [threshold]
description: Elastic threshold companion for rules/sigma/net_zeek_ssh_session_cadence.yml (issue #332, found during #261's security-auditor review). Alerts when a single source (source.ip) establishes >=5 SSH sessions (event.dataset:zeek.ssh, any client version-exchange banner Zeek parsed) within a 6-minute lookback (the real trigger is 5-in-6, not 5-in-5 - see the from/interval overlap note below). Reads zeek.ssh session records directly rather than the aggregated notice.log SSH::Password_Guessing/Login_By_Password_Guesser detect-bruteforcing.zeek fires on (30 failed auths / 30 minutes, both upstream Zeek defaults) - complementary coverage for the recall gap below that threshold, not a replacement for it. HONEST FRAMING (security-auditor finding): 5-in-6-minutes and 30-in-30-minutes are the SAME steady-state rate (~1 session/minute) - this rule improves DETECTION LATENCY for a burst-shaped attack and drops the dependency on auth_success, but does not lower the sustained rate an attacker can stay under to evade both rules indefinitely; a genuinely lower-rate long-window companion is a distinct, separate piece of work. Deliberately does not depend on auth_success: live-verified (client and server on separate docker network namespaces over a real bridge network, not loopback) that Zeek's auth_success field is entirely absent (not false) on failed-auth ssh.log records - tests/anomaly_simulation/verify_detections.py's own comment documents this same unreliability specifically over loopback (large MTU defeats Zeek's packet-size auth-outcome heuristic); this rule's own verification independently reproduced the identical symptom over a different topology. The Sigma file is the documented logic-of-record (single-session definition, including a documented known-limitation note on SSH::Info$client being &optional on a lossy capture vantage); this threshold rule adds the per-source count that sigma_eval.py / the lucene conversion target cannot express. Lookback window ("from": "now-6m") deliberately exceeds the run interval ("interval": "5m") so consecutive evaluations overlap by 1 minute - a non-overlapping (tumbling) 5m/5m window would let an attacker straddle two scheduled runs and stay under threshold in either one, the same reasoning the Windows 4625 threshold companion (auth-win-bruteforce-failed-logons.ndjson) already documents (that file's own 1-minute-overlap claim has the same known incompleteness this one does - true sliding-window coverage needs lookback >= interval + window; tracked as a follow-up against both files, not fixed one-sided here). Reads zeek.ssh, a genuinely different dataset than the pipeline's zeek.notice-driven T1110 tag, so neither path double-counts the same document - but a single high-volume attack can legitimately trip both, and metric_raw_alert_volume() sums its two sub-counts into one combined value even though it reports them separately too. This rule's alerts are NOT wired to SOAR dispatch (the /alert trigger gates on a threat.technique.id the zeek.notice path sets, not this one) - do not close that gap by tagging threat.technique.id on zeek.ssh documents directly, which would fire the unrate-limited /alert webhook once per real SSH session. KNOWN GAP (see the Sigma file's own description): a per-source.ip threshold cannot catch a genuinely distributed attack (many sources, each individually under threshold) - out of scope for this rule, tracked as a distinct piece of work.
author: Suburban-SOC
false_positives: An admin or automation tool (Ansible, deployment scripts, health checks) establishing several sequential SSH connections to the same host within a short window - legitimate session-reconnect patterns can resemble low-volume brute-force cadence at this threshold.
A jump host or bastion legitimately proxying multiple real users' sessions from one apparent source IP.
